profile.summary: VespaG predicts the effect of missense single amino acid substitutions in a protein from its sequence alone. It embeds the sequence with the protein language model ESM-2 and passes the per-residue embedding through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer of 256 units, which outputs a score for each of the 20 amino acids at each position. Because experimental variant data is scarce, the network was not trained on measurements: it was trained to reproduce the scores of the alignment-based predictor GEMME on 39 million variants of the human proteome. The authors report a mean Spearman correlation of 0.48 plus or minus 0.02 on the 217 assays of the ProteinGym substitution benchmark, and say the whole mutational landscape of a proteome can be predicted in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.

summary_quotes.text: We introduce VespaG, a blazingly fast missense amino acid variant effect predictor, leveraging protein language model (pLM) embeddings as input to a minimal deep learning model.

The method introduced in this work, VespaG, is a feed-forward neural network (FNN) with one hidden layer with 256 hidden units solely inputting sequence embeddings from the protein language model (pLM) ESM-2
we created a dataset of 39 million single amino acid variants from the human proteome applying the multiple sequence alignment-based effect predictor GEMME as a pseudo standard-of-truth
VespaG achieved a mean Spearman correlation of 0.48 ± 0.02, matching top-performing methods evaluated on the same data.

predicting all mutational landscapes of all proteins in proteomes such as <italic toggle="yes">Homo sapiens</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila melanogaster</italic> in under 30 min on a consumer laptop (12-core CPU, 16 GB RAM)

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is embedded by a frozen protein language model. The default is ESM-2, specifically esm2_t36_3B_UR50D as the README names it; the pretrained language models were used as is, without fine tuning. Each residue's embedding goes through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer, 256 hidden units and dropout of 0.2, which outputs a substitution score for every amino acid at that position. The training target was not experimental data. For about 5000 human proteins, homologous sequences were aligned with the MMseqs2-based strategy of ColabFold, GEMME was run on each alignment to produce a complete substitution matrix of size L by 20 with scores from minus 10 to 2, and the network was trained to map embeddings to those scores. The authors describe this as a student learning from an expert teacher, and compared the one-hidden-layer network against a linear regression, a two-layer network and a small convolutional network before settling on it.

We trained VespaG on a set of about 5000 human proteins to learn a mapping between the input pLM embeddings and the evolutionary scores computed by GEMME.

GEMME outputs a complete substitution matrix of dimension <italic toggle="yes">L</italic> × 20, with <italic toggle="yes">L</italic> being the length (in residue) of the input query protein sequence. GEMME scores range from −10 to 2.

We built the predictors with the following architectures: (1) Linear regression, i.e. a feed-forward neural network (FNN, <xref rid="btae621-B26" ref-type="bibr">LeCun <italic toggle="yes">et al.</italic> 2015</xref>) without any hidden layer, dubbed <italic toggle="yes">LinReg</italic>; (2) FNN with one dense hidden layer, called <italic toggle="yes">VespaG</italic>

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The weights ship inside the repository, not on a model hub. At the commit read here model_weights holds three files: v1/esm2.pt, v2/esm2.pt and v2/prott5.pt. The code sets the model version to v2 and loads model_weights/v2/<embedding type>.pt, with esm2 as the default embedding type, so a plain run uses v2/esm2.pt. The package version in pyproject.toml is 0.1.0. A result should therefore name the commit, the weight version folder and the embedding type, and also the language model used for the embeddings, since embeddings are either supplied by the user or generated at run time. What differs between v1 and v2 is not stated in the sources read. Retraining is possible: the repository drives it with DVC and offers precomputed embeddings and GEMME scores on Zenodo.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised missense variant effect predictor on top of frozen protein language model embeddings, trained against GEMME scores rather than experimental measurements.

quotes.text: We introduce VespaG, a blazingly fast missense amino acid variant effect predictor, leveraging protein language model (pLM) embeddings as input to a minimal deep learning model.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Feed-forward neural network with one hidden layer of 256 units and dropout 0.2, taking per-residue embeddings from a frozen language model as input.

quotes.text: VespaG, is a feed-forward neural network (FNN) with one hidden layer with 256 hidden units
"architecture": Architecture.fnn,

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A FASTA file of one or more protein sequences. Optionally precomputed ESM-2 (esm2_t36_3B_UR50D) embeddings, and optionally a CSV of specific mutations to score as rows of protein_id,mutation_id.

quotes.text: `--input/-i`: Path to FASTA-formatted file containing protein sequence(s).
`--mutation-file`: CSV file specifying specific mutations to score (expects rows of `protein_id,mutation_id`).

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: A score for each requested substitution, or for the whole single-site mutational landscape when no mutation file is given, written as a CSV per protein, optionally one CSV for all proteins or an HDF5 file, and optionally rescaled to the interval 0 to 1.

quotes.text: If not provided, the whole single-site mutational landscape of all input proteins will be scored.
`--h5-output`: Whether a file containing predictions in HDF5 format should be created.
`--normalize`: Whether to transform predicted scores to [0, 1] interval

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: About 660,000 trainable parameters, as the paper states ("660k free parameters"), for a network with one hidden layer of 256 units on 2560-dimensional ESM-2 embeddings. The frozen ESM-2 model that makes the embeddings has 3 billion parameters and is a separate download. The shipped files are 2,644,593 bytes for v2/esm2.pt and 1,071,729 bytes for v2/prott5.pt.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: 39 million single amino acid variants from the human proteome, labelled with GEMME scores rather than experiments, taken from about 5000 human proteins. Proteins shorter than 25 or longer than 1024 residues were removed, the set was redundancy reduced against the test data and against itself, and split 80/20 into training and validation. Further sets for Drosophila melanogaster, Escherichia coli and viruses were also built.

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: Two weight versions ship in the repository: v1 with an ESM-2 checkpoint, and v2 with an ESM-2 and a ProtT5 checkpoint. The code loads v2 by default with the ESM-2 embedding type. The Python package is version 0.1.0.

strengths.text: Fast and light once embeddings exist: the authors report predicting all mutational landscapes of a proteome in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.

quotes.text: VespaG has the advantage of being orders of magnitude faster, predicting all mutational landscapes of all proteins in proteomes such as <italic toggle="yes">Homo sapiens</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila melanogaster</italic> in under 30 min on a consumer laptop (12-core CPU, 16 GB RAM).

strengths.text: Prediction needs no alignment at run time. The alignments were used only to make the GEMME training labels.

strengths.text: The authors say the setup is easily retrainable with a new or updated language model, and the repository ships a DVC pipeline plus Zenodo embeddings and GEMME scores so that retraining can be repeated.

quotes.text: This setup increases interpretability compared to the baseline pLM and is easily retrainable with novel or updated pLMs.

strengths.text: The evaluation can be rerun from the repository: an eval subcommand downloads the ProteinGym reference and score files and computes Spearman correlation per assay.

quotes.text: You can reproduce our evaluation using the `eval` subcommand, which pre-processes data into a format usable by VespaG, runs `predict`, and computes performance metrics.

run_guide.summary: Install the package, clone the repository for its weights and example data, and score the example FASTA file.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or newer, as pyproject.toml requires.
A virtual environment, which the README asks for as step 0.
Enough patience or a GPU for the ESM-2 embedding step if no precomputed embeddings are supplied: the README warns that CPU embedding is slow.
GPL-3.0 applies to the code. The weights are committed in the same repository, with no separate licence statement.

limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The predict command looks for the weights under model_weights relative to the working directory, so it must be run from the cloned repository unless a checkpoint file is passed.
Reproducing the ProteinGym evaluation is a separate subcommand, vespag eval proteingym, which downloads the benchmark files.

notes: The repository address is written github.com/jschlensok/vespag in the paper and README and JSchlensok/VespaG by GitHub; they are the same repository and the pinned raw files use the GitHub spelling. The weights are committed in the repository rather than on a model hub; the repository licence is GPL-3.0 and there is no separate weights licence statement, so weights_licence is null. The paper gives 660k parameters for the ESM-2 network without naming the weight folder; v1/esm2.pt and v2/esm2.pt have the same size, so both carry that count. The difference between the v1 and v2 weight folders is not documented in the sources read, and the paper does not say which folder produced its numbers. The Zenodo deposit of training data was not fetched.
